An interval is a pair of endpoints,
; in most interview problems both ends are included, a

, where two intervals that share an end point already overlap. The technique behind almost every interval problem is sorting by one endpoint and then walking the sorted list once, keeping only a small amount of state as you go, most often the last block merged so far.

The problem is deciding which intervals overlap without comparing every pair against every other, an O(n²) check. Once the intervals are sorted by start, an interval can only ever touch the block that comes immediately before it, because every interval further along starts even later and cannot reach backward into an earlier block, so comparing against everything collapses into comparing against one thing.

The mechanism is a sweep with one invariant: the merged blocks stay disjoint and in the order they were sorted, and only the last one can still grow. For each interval in start order, if it starts at or before the last block's end the two overlap and the block's end becomes the larger of the two ends; otherwise the interval starts a fresh block. Counting instead of merging keeps the same shape with a running total in place of a block, and choosing the largest set of intervals that don't overlap at all sorts by end instead, because the interval that finishes first leaves the most room for the rest.

What goes wrong under pressure is two things. Assigning the new interval's end instead of taking the larger of the two ends passes every test where intervals only touch at an edge, and only fails once one interval sits entirely inside another and the assignment shrinks the block around it. And mixing the closed convention with a half-open one changes both the overlap test and the merge test: two closed intervals sharing an endpoint overlap and merge, but two half-open ones meeting at the same point don't overlap, even though they still merge into one contiguous block. When the sweep meets an interval that starts after the last block ends, every later interval starts later still, so none of them can reach back into that block, and the block is final. This is the sweep's invariant: the merged blocks are disjoint and in order, every interval seen so far lies inside one of them, and only the last block can still grow. Say it in an interview, because "sort first, and explain why" is what the question tests. The cost is the sort, O(n log n). The sweep itself is O(n).
